question: Which sequent says that $P$ and $Q$ cannot both hold?
options: $P, Q \Rightarrow$
$\Rightarrow P, Q$
$P \lor Q \Rightarrow$
$\Rightarrow \neg P, Q$
explanation: Formulas on the left are read together, and an empty succedent says the antecedent is contradictory. $P \lor Q \Rightarrow$ says something stronger, that neither holds, while $\Rightarrow P, Q$ asserts $P \lor Q$, since commas on the right are read disjunctively.

question: Which sequent would become provable if the eigenvariable condition were dropped?
options: $\forall x P(x) \Rightarrow P(a)$
$P(a) \Rightarrow \exists x P(x)$
$P(a) \Rightarrow \forall x P(x)$
$\exists x P(x) \Rightarrow \exists x P(x)$
explanation: From the axiom $P(a) \Rightarrow P(a)$, Right $\forall$ would generalise on $a$ even though $a$ occurs in the antecedent, licensing the move from one case to all. The other three are provable with the condition in force, since Left $\forall$ and Right $\exists$ may use any term.

question: A cut-free proof of $\Rightarrow Q \rightarrow (P \rightarrow P)$ in LK must use which structural rule?
options: Contraction, to merge two occurrences of $P$ on the left of the arrow
Weakening, to bring in $Q$ as an assumption that is never used
Contraction, to merge two copies of $P \rightarrow P$ on the right of the arrow
None, since the logical rules for the conditional suffice on their own
explanation: Working backwards, Right $\rightarrow$ twice leaves $Q, P \Rightarrow P$, and the axiom has only $P$ on the left, so $Q$ must be added by weakening. This is the step relevance logic refuses: dropping weakening blocks conclusions that ignore their premises.

question: Why is cut, alone among the rules, an obstacle to searching backwards for a proof?
options: It has two premises, so the search tree branches at every cut that is tried
It is the only rule that moves a formula from one side of the arrow to the other
It can be applied only after weakening has been used on both of its premises
Its conclusion does not reveal the cut formula, so any formula might be needed
explanation: Every other rule's premises can be read off its conclusion, built from what the conclusion contains; after a cut the vanished formula could have been anything. Two premises are not the problem, since Right $\land$ and Left $\lor$ have two and leave search finite, and the negation rules also move formulas across the arrow.

question: A proof cuts on $\varphi \land \psi$. The left premise came by Right $\land$ from proofs of $\Gamma \Rightarrow \varphi$ and $\Gamma \Rightarrow \psi$, and the right premise by Left $\land$ from $\varphi, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$. What does the reduction step do?
options: Cuts the proof of $\Gamma \Rightarrow \varphi$ against that of $\varphi, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$, dropping the proof of $\psi$
Cuts first on $\varphi$ and then on $\psi$, keeping both halves of the proof of the left premise
Moves the cut above the Right $\land$ rule, leaving the cut formula as $\varphi \land \psi$ itself
Removes the cut and weakens the proof of $\Gamma \Rightarrow \varphi$ into a proof of $\Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta$
explanation: The conjunction was built on one side only to be taken apart on the other, so the detour is deleted and the cut falls to a simpler formula. The proof of $\psi$ was never needed; moving a cut upward without simplifying it is the other kind of step, used only when a premise does not act on the cut formula.

question: Because cut is admissible, a cut-free proof of a sequent is never vastly longer than a proof of it that uses cuts.
options: True
False
explanation: Admissibility concerns what is provable, not at what length: eliminating cuts can enlarge a proof by more than any tower of exponentials of fixed height. Lemmas are how proofs stay short, and the theorem's uses are uses of the possibility, not of the transformation.

question: How do cut elimination and the subformula property show that the empty sequent has no proof?
options: Every axiom is true under every interpretation, so no derivation can ever reach a false sequent
The empty sequent has no subformulas, so no cut on any of its formulas can be performed
A cut-free proof of it could hold only subformulas of nothing, hence no formulas and no axioms
Contraction cannot shrink a sequent to nothing, so every proof must end with a non-empty one
explanation: Any proof can be made cut-free, and every formula in a cut-free proof is a subformula of the end sequent, which here has none; a proof with no formulas has no axioms at its leaves. The appeal to interpretations is soundness, a semantic argument, whereas this one inspects only the shape of proofs.

question: $P \land Q$ implies $Q \lor R$. Which formula is an interpolant for that implication?
options: $P \land Q$
$Q \lor R$
explanation: An interpolant may use only vocabulary common to both sides, which here is just $Q$, and $P \land Q$ implies $Q$, which implies $Q \lor R$. Taking either given formula as its own interpolant fails, since each contains a letter, $P$ or $R$, that the other lacks.

question: On the article's account, what does Gentzen's consistency proof for arithmetic establish?
options: That arithmetic is consistent on the basis of pure logic alone, by eliminating every cut
That arithmetic's consistency follows from induction up to epsilon zero, which arithmetic cannot prove
That arithmetic proves its own consistency once the induction rule is treated as a kind of cut
That cuts on induction formulas can be eliminated, giving arithmetic the subformula property
explanation: Induction behaves like cut and cannot simply be eliminated, so Gentzen assigns ordinals to proofs and relies on the well-foundedness of the ordering below epsilon zero. That assumption is the exact price: arithmetic proves well-foundedness for every shorter ordering but not this one, as the second incompleteness theorem requires.

question: The LK derivation of $\Rightarrow P \lor \neg P$ is blocked in LJ. Where, and why?
options: At line 2, because two formulas stand in the succedent
At line 5, because LJ has no contraction rule at all
At line 3, because LJ lacks the right rule for disjunction
At line 2, because LJ has no right rule for negation
explanation: Every rule used is also an LJ rule; what LJ forbids is the format, a second formula on the right, which first appears at line 2. Nothing was added to obtain classical logic: the extra room in the succedent is what buys excluded middle.
